title: Lambic and Gueuze Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: How spontaneous fermentation and years in an oak barrel turn plain wort into lambic, and why gueuze is a blend rather than a recipe.
teaser: No yeast is pitched. The beer ferments with whatever the air around Brussels happens to carry in.
standfirst: Lambic is the style that breaks the first rule most brewers are taught, that you choose your yeast. It is left to spontaneous fermentation instead, and gueuze is what a blender builds from the results.
sections: A beer nobody pitches yeast into

Lambic is brewed in the Payottenland region around Brussels using a technique that predates the whole idea of a pure yeast culture. After the boil, the hot wort is run into a wide, shallow, open vessel called a coolship overnight, exposed to the open air. Whatever wild yeast and bacteria are present in that air and in the brewery's own timbers settle into the wort and begin fermenting it, entirely uncontrolled and unchosen.

The beer is then aged in oak barrels, called foeders, for one to three years, during which a shifting population of organisms, principally Brettanomyces yeast alongside Lactobacillus and Pediococcus bacteria, work through the beer in overlapping waves and leave it dry, tart and intensely complex.

Lambic uses hops in a way that looks almost backwards to a modern brewer: aged hops, deliberately stored until most of their aroma and a good share of their bitterness have faded. The hops are there for their mild antibacterial effect during the long ageing process, not for flavour. A lambic should never taste hoppy.

The grain bill typically includes a large proportion of unmalted wheat, often 30 to 40 percent, alongside barley malt, giving the finished beer a slightly grainy, almost lemony backbone under the sourness.
Gueuze is a blender's craft, not a recipe

Straight lambic is rarely bottled on its own. Gueuze is made by blending young lambic, usually around a year old and still holding some fermentable sugar, with older lambic that has fully dried out and matured for two or three years. The blend is bottled and left to referment, driven by the sugar still present in the young component, which builds natural carbonation over several more months.

Getting that blend right is a skill closer to winemaking than brewing. The blender is tasting dozens of barrels, each one behaving slightly differently, and deciding which combination will produce a balanced, lively finished beer rather than something flat or unpleasantly sharp.
What is actually in the glass

Lambic and gueuze are pale straw to light gold, highly carbonated in the bottled gueuze form, and dry to the point of almost no perceived sweetness. Acidity is the dominant character, closer to a dry cider or a sharp white wine than to any other beer style, with barnyard, hay and sometimes a light lemon or green apple note layered underneath.
A brewhouse detail that shows the risk involved

Because the fermentation depends on whatever organisms happen to be present, a single batch can fail outright, developing an unpleasant vinegar sharpness or a flat, uninteresting character if the wrong balance of wild yeast and bacteria takes hold that year. Traditional lambic producers accept that some barrels will simply not be good enough to bottle, which is baked into how the whole style is priced and produced.
Where this fits for a curious drinker

Lambic and gueuze sit at the sour end of the same Belgian tradition that produces Flanders red ale, and tasting the two side by side is a good way to understand the difference between spontaneous fermentation and a controlled mixed culture. Serve cool, around 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, in a tulip glass, and approach it the way you would a sharp, dry wine rather than a typical beer.
A tradition that is genuinely hard to copy

Producers outside the Payottenland region have tried, with limited success, to recreate true lambic elsewhere, since so much of the character depends on the specific mix of organisms resident in that particular area's air and in decades old brewery timbers. What travels more easily is the general technique, coolship cooling, long barrel ageing and blending, which shows up in mixed fermentation beers from breweries around the world, even when the exact result cannot be called lambic in the traditional sense. Understanding why that copying is so hard is itself a useful lesson in how much of brewing depends on the specific place it happens, not only the recipe on paper.

Some breweries elsewhere shortcut the process by pitching a commercial blend of Brettanomyces and souring bacteria directly into a controlled tank rather than waiting for a coolship to do the work. The resulting beer can be genuinely enjoyable, but brewers who have tasted both alongside each other tend to agree that it lacks the layered, slowly built complexity that years in oak and a truly wild starting culture provide.
faqs: Why is no yeast added when brewing lambic?

The wort is deliberately exposed to open air in a shallow vessel so that wild yeast and bacteria present in the local environment settle in and ferment it, a technique called spontaneous fermentation.
What is the difference between lambic and gueuze?
Lambic is the base beer aged in oak barrels. Gueuze is a blend of young and old lambic, bottled together so that residual sugar in the young component drives a second fermentation and carbonation.
Why does lambic use old, stale hops instead of fresh ones?

Aged hops keep a mild antibacterial effect useful during long barrel ageing while contributing almost no bitterness or aroma, which keeps the beer's flavour focused on the fermentation character rather than the hops.
